findings.title: Debug logging left at Error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: The new cleanup loops log every batch at Error level and include the full `ids` slice. These calls are at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. A batch can hold tens of thousands of IDs, so each run floods the logs with huge Error entries even when nothing went wrong. That breaks error alerting and inflates log volume. These look like leftover debug statements; remove them or lower them to Debug without the ID list.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute while job timeout is still 9 minutes
findings.body: The global cleanup interval drops from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This change is unrelated to the deadlock fix and looks like leftover debugging. Every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, and so on) now runs ten times as often. That adds database load and makes contention with inserts more likely, which works against the goal of this PR. The per-run timeout is still 9 minutes, much longer than the new interval, so the timeout no longer matches the schedule. Revert to 10 minutes.

findings.title: SQLite parameter-limit check uses configured batch size instead of actual ID count
findings.body: The code decides whether to inline IDs based on `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize`, not on `len(ids)`. When the batch size is above 999 it always inlines, which is safe but inconsistent with the stated reason. The check also assumes no other code path ever passes more IDs than the batch size. Base the decision on `len(ids)`. In addition, building the inlined list with repeated `fmt.Sprintf` copies the whole string on every ID, which is quadratic for 32k IDs. Use `strings.Builder` or `strconv` instead.

findings.title: MaxCount cleanup can loop indefinitely under concurrent inserts
findings.body: Each MaxCount batch re-runs `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount` and keeps looping while rows are deleted. While annotations keep being inserted, every new row pushes an older row past the offset, so the loop may never see zero affected rows. Only the 9-minute context timeout would stop it, and it runs one SELECT and one DELETE per batch the whole time. The old single-statement version behaved the same way, but the extra round trip per batch makes it costlier. Consider capping the number of iterations.
